chapters.title: Welcome Back — These Courses Are Not University Classes

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: Good afternoon. Good morning, good afternoon — welcome back. All of you online, turn on your cameras. Come on, stop hiding. Don't be shy — your faces are all so beautiful. Great, we got two people to turn on the camera. And Marina never sleeps — I told her to do something at night, and she doesn't do it, and then in the morning she sleeps for me. She's getting a little red. Nothing like embarrassing a student. We don't think she sleeps — we actually suspect she wasn't sleeping at all.

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: So welcome back. Last night's class was a lot of fun — for me, anyway. I've taught these courses several times, and each time I teach it, some new information or new idea comes out.

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: These classes are not meant to be like a university class, where you take it once, you do the homework, you get a certificate, and then voilà, you're done. You continue spending time with the ideas over and over again.

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: I'm going to embarrass Marina again. She wrote me and said, "I'm done with my 18 ACI courses. What should I do next?" I said, "Do them again." She's like, "What?" I said, "Yeah, do it again." Because the first time through, you have a certain understanding. And then as you live the ideas, deeper and deeper understandings come. The ideas are not in the classes themselves — the words, the practices, they're just like maps. And then as you live it, the ideas become lived, integrated inside of you.

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: That's why you go to hours and hours of classes, and then you do it again and again. I know someone who's taking an anatomy course for the third time. Didn't you get it the first time? But each layer becomes more and more subtle. Your understanding becomes more and more integrated. These courses are like the anatomy of your life — the anatomy of your mind, the anatomy of your heart. Each time we go in, you're getting a different layer.

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: So each time I go into the course, I'm like, "Oh, that's interesting. That's interesting." And I teach it differently, in different ways. Even last night, I didn't expect the things that I said — because you draw the information out. What do you need? As I'm up here talking, I'm looking at each of you, and there's a lot of information being exchanged. Different ideas come together in those moments, and it becomes an organic learning for everybody. So thank you for teaching me.

chapters.title: Your First Teachers — Parents and the Seeds for a Teacher

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: Brian just gave a great meditation. He led you into a space of: how did you create your teachers? What seeds did you bring into this life that created the teachers that you have? And when you really think about it — who were your first teachers? This is where you're allowed to speak. Who were your first teachers?

paragraphs.speaker: Audience
paragraphs.text: Your parents.

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: Your parents, right. You were born into a place where you had people teaching you things right away, from the moment you're born. We don't think of our parents that way. Usually we think of our parents as these annoying people who are always telling us what to do. Right, Morgan? For those of you online who don't know — Morgan's mom is here, and his mom and dad are usually here in class, so I get to make fun of him too. Where are you, Morgan?

paragraphs.speaker: Morgan
paragraphs.text: I'm back at school, in Australia.

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: Australia. Sweet, thank you. Thank you for being here.

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: So they're teaching you from the very first moment. You came into this life — think of it — you may not like your parents now, or you might have issues with them. If you don't have issues with your parents, they weren't good parents. Because that's their job. Their job was to make you an independent human being. And it doesn't matter how old you get, your parents are still going to be your parents. Even if you've lost your parents, because of age or whatever reason, you never resolve that tension. That was their role in your life.

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: I saw this stand-up comic. I love comedy — I love watching and learning how other people deliver jokes, the people who can have an entire audience laughing for two hours. This one comic was talking about childbirth, and then she went off on a trip to talk about giraffes — what happens when a giraffe gives birth. The giraffe is super tall, and she doesn't sit down to give birth. The mom giraffe is basically standing up, and she gives birth, and the baby just falls to the ground. And she kind of looks at it, and she's like, "Get up! You gotta walk. You're going to die if you don't get up." And she just walks away. The baby giraffe's like, "Got to go." That's the teaching. If you don't walk away, you're going to get eaten. It was really funny — of course, when the comic did it, it was much funnier than when I do it. I'll see if I can find the video for the next class.

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: The giraffe has a teacher right away. But it's not gentle — it's not, "Let me help you, little baby." It's just, "Get up or die." When you came out of your mother, hopefully she was like, "Aww," and held you, and offered her breast to drink milk. And then she started teaching you things. You had somebody with you, whether you like them or not, for so long.

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: To the moms and dads of the world — congratulations. Everyone who becomes a parent suddenly realizes what their parents did for them. You go, "Oh… that's what Mom was doing. Oh my God, my parents didn't sleep for three years." As a child, all you do is — food, dirty diaper. That's all you do as a baby, and then your needs are taken care of. But you had those people in your life. You had that karma. You came into this life with the seeds to have a teacher. Don't forget that. Part of those meditations are to help us realize there were certain things going on that are incredibly important. And you should feel lucky. You should feel happy. And then — what are you going to do to ensure that you have those seeds for the next life?

chapters.title: Why We Do These Meditations — The KitKat Questions

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: So why are we doing that meditation? I'm sure Brian talked about this. Why do we care about revisiting our childbirth, our first couple of years, and thinking about the teachers who were forced upon us by the seeds we planted in the past?

paragraphs.speaker: Max
paragraphs.text: To know that we had those seeds, and to know what's coming in the future — what we'll become with these seeds.

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: Yes, but that's not the answer that gets the KitKat. Were you in the class with Brian? Did you listen to him at all? Did you forget?

paragraphs.speaker: Audience
paragraphs.text: A random guess — because there's a big event in October. It has to do with our meditation.

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: I want the why. Yes, Arlene.

paragraphs.speaker: Arlene
paragraphs.text: So we can replant those beautiful seeds, whether it's for this life or the next.

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: I'm eating the KitKat. I'm going to tell you the answer — you just wanted to see me eat the KitKat, huh? If you had paid attention to Brian's class, you too could be eating a KitKat.

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: There are three reasons. One of them is the one that Max and Arlene mentioned — understanding the seeds that brought you in and the seeds that are going to take you on. But there are two other, deeper meanings. One is to prepare our minds to start looking at things differently in the world. And yes — it has to do with October, like was mentioned. It has to do with the ways in which our practice changes as we move from sutra to the Diamond Way. Because it changes the things we grew up with — we had certain ideas about the way things were.

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: You were born into this life because your mom and dad — Morgan, cover your ears — had some fun time together. The sperm and egg came together, biologically speaking. All the different combinations came together, your genetic material came together, and then you came out, and you grew up and became an adult. We normally don't think about it — we just sort of think it happened that way. But in Diamond Way practice, we start thinking: what if the things that were happening to us were actually happening for a reason, for a higher reason? So we start revisiting our normal memories, looking for — well, maybe there was something special. Were your parents just normal, boring people raising you? Or were they teachers? And then you start asking, what kind of teachers? And you start revisiting things, step by step. All of a sudden you start considering all the things that happened to you that maybe weren't just normal, random things. You begin to suspect that maybe there was a divine plan — self-existently, from its own side? No — somehow your seeds created it.

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: It's such a different way of thinking about things. And it's a hard path. At least for me and a couple of my friends, these meditations are not necessarily the easiest — because there could be things that happened to you that weren't pleasant, and you have to start looking at those things again, with a different lens.

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: Now, the third reason these meditations are preparation for the Diamond Way course that's already kind of started — what else do they do? Another KitKat bar. Who taught these meditations?

paragraphs.speaker: Audience
paragraphs.text: Geshe Michael.

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: Geshe Michael — very good. But that does not get you the KitKat. Why did he teach them? They're preparations for something.

paragraphs.speaker: Audience
paragraphs.text: Because his teacher also taught him that way.

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: Not quite. Not incorrect, but not quite. Yes?

paragraphs.speaker: Audience
paragraphs.text: It has to do with kōngxìng (空性) — emptiness. You can see emptiness directly.

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: That's close enough. They're preparations to see emptiness directly. The trajectory that Geshe Michael is taking us on — taking us into Diamond Way practice — he's already doing it through the lens of how to prepare to see emptiness directly. All the preparation we've been going through with him is geared toward that. Everything we're doing right now really boils down to: can you get to that experience? Can you plant the seeds so that you could generate that experience and understand where things are coming from — so that you can truly help all living beings?

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: All the different courses, all the different topics, all the different angles we're taking are just pieces to guide you toward that experience — to create the conditions for wisdom to arise. Whatever resonates with you the most, that's what Geshe Michael cares about the most.

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: So with these meditations — the first one is: let's think about our early teachers. We understand that we're already being taken care of because we took care of other people in the past. And understanding that relationship is a step toward understanding how to see emptiness directly. And it keeps building from there. What we're conveniently doing this week is looking at all the things that we don't want to be, so that we can create the conditions to actually exit from this cycle of suffering.

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: So this course builds an entire argument: here are all these different kinds of beings in the universe, and why you don't want to be them, and what the causes are to become them. And then you have to look at your life and go, "Oops." That's the whole point of this course. First, to recognize the beauty and the incredible seeds that were planted to create this opportunity. And to ensure that you continue this upward spiral — whether you do it in this lifetime, or the next, or over the next 20 lifetimes. As long as you're going up, it doesn't matter.

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: The depressing part of this course is that you're probably going to be like, "Oh, I've done those things." And it's okay. Don't worry if you're like, "I may have done some of those things." The idea is: how do we purify it, and how do we get ourselves onto a different track?

chapters.title: Review — The Form Realm and Its Seventeen Levels

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: Okay, we'll do a bit of a review. Next slide, Brian — number two. This is the form realm. Repeat after me — suk, suk [GZUGS]. Don't make it a hard Z, even though there's a Z written up there. It's not "zuka" — so don't read the Z as an English Z; it's an English S.

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: So Janet and I had an argument one day about whether the tones in Tibetan are similar to the tones in Chinese. We got to the point where it's like — it depends how you're learning it. We didn't resolve it; they're different languages. But if it helps you to understand it through tones: in Tibetan they have two tones, high and low. You just have to know what the difference is.

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: The idea here is that this realm, the form realm, is above us — it's higher than the desire realm around us. It has four different parts. And I made it easy for you to remember — I did a little ChatGPT for you on a slide. So there are four parts. How many sections does the first part have?

paragraphs.speaker: Audience
paragraphs.text: Three.

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: How many parts does the second one have?

paragraphs.speaker: Audience
paragraphs.text: Three.

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: Great. The third one?

paragraphs.speaker: Audience
paragraphs.text: Three.

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: And the fourth one?

paragraphs.speaker: Audience
paragraphs.text: Eight.

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: Eight. For a total of 17. So there's your ChatGPT. I did not use ChatGPT — I can do that myself. But that's just to help you remember.
